460.t: Wes Montgomery, Don Sebesky and Jimmy Smith dates
460.s: Laws did not know he was on Wes Montgomery's Down Here on the Ground, probably via Creed Taylor. Brown lists Sebesky's and Jimmy Smith's dates.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: I didn’t know I played on that. I know that record. I’ve heard it. But I didn’t know I played on it.

460.t: Milt Jackson, Roy Ayers and Helen Merrill sessions
460.s: Brown lists sessions with Milt Jackson, Roy Ayers and Helen Merrill. Laws vaguely recalls some and not others.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: I didn’t know I played with him. I don’t remember playing the record with him.

460.t: Walter Wanderley, Milton Nascimento and Moondog
460.s: Brown lists sessions with Walter Wanderley, Milton Nascimento and Moondog. Laws remembers some under Creed Taylor and admits to having forgotten many.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: Moondog used to play on the streets, in the subways and stuff. But I don’t remember doing a session with him.

460.s: Brown mentions a Melvin Sparks date at Van Gelder's; Laws does not know him.
460.ch: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
460.q: Sorry. It doesn’t ring a bell. It must have been just one experience.

460.t: The Mingus Let My Children Hear Music credit
460.s: Brown notes Lord lists Laws on a 1971 Mingus date. Laws suggests he played a Sebesky chart without knowing it was Mingus's record.
460.ch: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
460.q: It may have been a Don Sebesky-type thing where he wrote the chart, and I came in and played it without knowing it was a Mingus record.

460.s: Laws recalls a Helen Merrill session at the Riverside studios and Mongo's last records there.
460.q: I remember Helen Merrill. I remember we recorded up in Riverside – what used to be Riverside recording studios. That’s where Orrin used to be also. I recorded up there with Mongo. Mongo did one of his last records up there at Riverside, along with Nat Adderley playing trumpet on a tune that I wrote…

460.t: Crying Song, the Gary McFarland date and guitarist Sam Brown
460.s: Brown dates Crying Song to September 1969. Laws identifies a garbled name in the discography as guitarist Sam Brown.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: You know what? I don’t think Sam Brown had that problem, because he wasn’t signed to any label. But he was a fine guitarist. He played both electric and acoustic guitars. He used to be on all the sessions. Every time you’d go, you’d see Sam playing on those sessions.

460.t: Bobby Timmons's Got to Get It
460.s: Laws does not recall a Bobby Timmons date but suspects Tom McIntosh recruited him. He says he often plays Timmons's tune Dat Dere.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: I play his tune all the time. I just played it the other night. Dat Dere. We played that, recorded it. We played it the other night.

460.t: Ron Carter, George Benson, Mongo's Stone Soul and Ernie Wilkins
460.s: Brown reads through late 1969 and early 1970s dates; Laws recalls the Ernie Wilkins session playing sax and flute.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: Yeah, I played sax and flute. It was kind of hard stuff going on in there.

460.s: Brown names the Milt Jackson CTI quintet date; Laws can't recall it.
460.q: I just don’t recall that session.

460.t: First Mongo recording at the Village Gate and other early dates
460.s: Laws says the Village Gate music felt familiar, and that Mongo already had a hit with Watermelon Man. He says he has forgotten many early sessions.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: Absolutely. It was nothing different from what I was accustomed to playing before. It was like when I played with the Jazz Crusaders. I wasn’t playing with the Jazz Crusaders. I played with the name before that, the Swingsters. But you know what group I’m talking about. No, the music was no…

460.t: The Swinger from Rio sessions and Lord's discography
460.s: Laws recalls flamboyant flute on Sergio Mendes's The Swinger from Rio. Brown shows him Tom Lord's discography with its 333 entries.
460.ch: Mongo Santamaria and early recording sessions
460.q: I remember that. Nesuhi was so impressed. I just did some little flamboyant stuff on the flute that anybody could do, and he’s just flipping. But see, here again, the right

460.t: Norman Connors's Love from the Sun
460.s: Brown lists personnel on Norman Connors's all-star record; Laws does not recall it.

505.t: Mr. Jones date with Elvin Jones
505.s: Liebman recalls the many percussionists on the July 1972 Mr. Jones sessions and is unsure which tunes were recorded that day.
505.q: I seem to remember that some of the tunes were from maybe another date. I don’t remember. Mr. Jones is not a – I don’t think we sat and did it. That’s a lot of percussionists there. Frank Ippolito was there.

505.t: Link Chamberlain's record and Kikuchi's Japanese Miles-inspired date
505.s: They recall playing on Link Chamberlain's leader date and Masabumi Kikuchi's On the Corner-style record, part of his run of Japanese dates.
505.q: Kikuchi, he’s first generation that. That was definitely that. That was when I started to do a lot of Japanese dates. I was hot in Japan for a minute, a couple of records, Japan.

505.t: First Visit in Japan, Abbey Lincoln, Spirit in the Sky and Drum Ode dates
505.s: They run through his first Japan record date, the Abbey Lincoln session, Open Sky overdubs, Drum Ode's date, a Bob Moses big-band record, and trumpeter Mike Lawrence.
505.q: Yes, first time in Japan. Landed with Miles. Like it was in those days, you got off the plane, and you had a record date. It’s unbelievable. I did my first record as leader there, first visit. Stan Getz was there, and who was in the band? Richie, Dave, and Jack. So that’s how First Visit came…

505.t: Terumasa Hino's Journey to Air session
505.s: Kirchner reads the personnel of Hino's 1970 New York session, which Liebman likens to Ascension.
505.q: Okay. We’re all in the studio together. I think the whole thing is Ascension. That’s a free – because Hino would come over and do something with American musicians. Upsurge Studios, 55 West 19th Street, Tom Di Pietro.

223.t: Discography check: Rosolino date and the Woody Herman session
223.s: Brown reads the Rosolino and March 1954 Woody Herman entries; Holman remembers none of the titles.
223.q: I don‟t remember any of those titles.

223.t: Terry Gibbs's More Vibes on Velvet
223.s: Holman does not recall this Pete Rugolo-arranged November 1958 date and mentions Gibbs's own band from 1959.
223.q: This date, I don‟t know anything about. I don‟t remember Pete writing for Terry. I think it was only the sax section – sax section and rhythm. I remember he did some dates with that combination, but I don‟t recall that particular one.

223.t: Bobby Troup and His Stars of Jazz date
223.s: Brown lists the all-star Victor date; Holman can only say Stars of Jazz was a television show.
223.q: Stars of Jazz was a t.v. show. I guess Bobby was the host for a while. I‟m just trying to figure out if that could have been a t.v. show or a recording date. I really can‟t say.

494.t: Sideman dates: Joe Henderson's The Kicker and Hutcherson's Now
494.s: Relaxed Joe Henderson date with Ron Carter and Louis Hayes, and Hutcherson's Now.
494.q: Oh yeah. Joe Henderson. Wow, what a – Joe Henderson was amazing. I was really flattered to get that call to do the recording. Again, it was just very, very relaxed. It was Ron Carter. I’m trying to remember who the drummer was – Louis Hayes. Yeah,

85.t: Recordings with Mezz Mezzrow, Charlie Barnet and Bud Freeman
85.s: Berger runs through Carter's 1933-34 sideman sessions; Carter has forgotten several, including the Bud Freeman date with Willie the Lion and Chick Webb.
85.q: Yeah, I think that’s the only . . . I’ve seen him a number of times, particularly when we went to Europe, and I think he was living in England for a while. Yeah, gee.

506.t: Wes Montgomery's So Much Guitar session
506.s: Carter explains why being called for Wes's record, with no music and a flugelhorn player, was a milestone.
506.q: Well then, you know, he'd made records with other bass players: Sam and probably Percy. I never played with Hank Jones. I hadn't met Hank Jones before and didn't know Ray Baretto. I think I met Lex Humphries somewhere. But they're all strangers. And I know Orrin Keepnews had his cadre of musicians…

136.t: Her Storyville recordings in New York for George Wein
136.s: Brown checks the discography; she cut two sessions, with Chambers and Thigpen and with Haynes and Pettiford.
136.ch: Boston, Berklee and New York encounters
136.q: ‟56, I don‟t know, George Wein was at that time music director, A&R man for Storyville recordings. So, we did two recordings in New York. One was [with] Paul Chambers—Miles had some kind of problem with his throat, and they weren‟t working— so Paul Chambers and Ed. Another one was with Roy Haynes…

167.t: Kicking off tunes and keeping the hungover players straight
167.s: The others depended on Bunn to start the tunes; he was tired of being called to keep things straight, and he cannot recall where "If You See Me Coming" came from.
167.ch: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
167.q: The first thing they'd do is say, "Get Teddy Bunn, get Teddy Bunn, get Teddy Bunn. He'll keep it straight. He'll keep it straight."
